technical: An orchestration pattern that decomposes a task into stages such as planning, execution, criticism and revision, distributed across one or more model instances with defined roles and handoffs. Compared with a fully autonomous single loop, constraining the graph of permitted transitions improves reliability and auditability, at the cost of flexibility on tasks the designer did not anticipate.
intuitive: Breaking work into defined steps with checks between them, rather than letting one model improvise the whole thing. It resembles a clinical pathway: less adaptable than free judgement, but far easier to inspect when it goes wrong.
clinical: A draft, review and attending sign-off structure maps cleanly onto this pattern and keeps a human at the point of consequence.

technical: Partitioning source documents into passages sized for embedding and retrieval, balancing granularity against coherence. Small chunks improve retrieval precision but sever context needed for interpretation; large chunks preserve context but dilute the embedding across multiple topics. Strategies include fixed-token windows with overlap, structure-aware splitting on headings, and semantic splitting at topic boundaries.
intuitive: Cutting long documents into passages small enough to search. Where you cut matters a great deal: split a note between the finding and its qualifier and the system can retrieve a fragment whose meaning is the opposite of the original.
clinical: A chunk boundary that separates a result from its negation, such as no evidence of, is a well-documented way for retrieval systems to surface dangerously misleading passages.

technical: Mapping text to fixed-length dense vectors with a trained encoder, then ranking by a similarity metric over those vectors. Encoders are typically trained with contrastive objectives so that semantically related pairs lie close together. Similarity is defined only relative to the training distribution of the encoder, so a general-purpose model may compress clinically important distinctions that were rare or unmarked in its training data.
intuitive: Turning each piece of text into a list of numbers that captures its meaning, then measuring which lists are closest together. What counts as close is decided by how the encoder was trained, so a model trained on web text may treat two clinically distinct conditions as nearly identical.
clinical: Off-the-shelf embeddings frequently place different stages or subtypes of a disease very close together, which degrades retrieval precision on exactly the distinctions that alter management.

technical: A protocol in which the caller supplies machine-readable declarations of available functions, including names, descriptions and parameter schemas, and the model emits a structured invocation naming a function and arguments rather than prose. The model does not execute anything: the host application validates and runs the call, then returns the result into the context for a subsequent turn.
intuitive: Giving the model a menu of buttons it may press, where pressing means writing a precise request that your own software then carries out. The model chooses and fills in the request; your code decides whether to honour it.
clinical: This is the seam where a chatbot becomes capable of ordering, querying a chart or messaging a patient, and therefore the natural place to put authorisation checks.

technical: Constraining a model's output to be supported by identifiable source material, and evaluating that support as an explicit property. Grounding is typically implemented by retrieving passages into context and then verified post hoc by decomposing the output into atomic claims and checking each against the cited source, since a citation being present is not evidence that it entails the sentence attached to it.
intuitive: Making the model show its work by pointing at the specific text it is relying on. Retrieval makes grounding possible but does not make it true: the model can still cite a real document that does not actually say what it claims.
clinical: The vendor claim that a tool is grounded in the guidelines or grounded in the chart is a claim about the retrieval step, not about entailment, so ask what fraction of generated statements were verified against their cited source and by whom, and check whether links point at the exact passage or at a document you then have to read yourself.

technical: Controls layered around a model to constrain inputs and outputs, including classifier-based input and output filters, schema and grammar constraints, retrieval scoping, allowlisted tool permissions, and rule engines governing dialogue flow. They are defence in depth around a model whose behaviour cannot be formally guaranteed, and each layer has its own false positive and false negative profile.
intuitive: Checks placed before and after the model, rather than inside it, because the model itself cannot be proved safe. Like any screening test they miss things and they also block legitimate requests, so tuning them is a trade-off rather than a fix.
clinical: Over-aggressive filters routinely block legitimate clinical queries about overdose thresholds, self-harm risk or controlled substances, which is a real usability and safety cost.

technical: A structured representation of entities as nodes and typed relations as edges, supporting multi hop traversal, constraint checking, and provenance on individual assertions. Combined with language models it is used either to supply retrieval targets with explicit relational structure or to validate generated claims against curated edges, trading the coverage of free text for auditability.
intuitive: Facts stored as explicit links between things rather than as sentences, so you can walk from a drug to its mechanism to a contraindicated condition and see each step. It knows less than the open web but can tell you exactly where each link came from.
clinical: Clinical medicine already runs on graphs, from SNOMED CT hierarchies to drug interaction and gene disease databases, and grounding a model against them is attractive precisely because each edge has a maintainer and a citation; the limit is coverage, since the graph only contains what someone curated.

technical: An open protocol standardising how model applications connect to external tools, data sources and prompts. A host application runs clients that speak JSON-RPC to servers exposing three primitives: tools, which are callable functions, resources, which are readable data, and prompts, which are reusable templates. It decouples integrations from any single vendor, so one server can serve any conforming client.
intuitive: A common plug shape between AI applications and the systems they need to reach. Instead of writing a bespoke connector for every combination of assistant and data source, a source exposes one server and any conforming assistant can use it.
clinical: Relevant to how a clinical assistant reaches an EHR or an imaging archive, and it is the layer where scoping and authorisation for that access should be enforced.

technical: An architecture that retrieves relevant passages from an external corpus at query time and conditions generation on them, so factual content comes from a non-parametric, updatable store rather than from weights. It reduces but does not eliminate fabrication: the model can still misread, over-generalise, or ignore retrieved evidence, and retrieval failures propagate silently into fluent output.
intuitive: Look it up, then answer, with the source text pasted into the prompt. It lets you update the knowledge base without retraining and lets you show citations, but if the search misses the right document the model will still answer confidently from memory.
clinical: This is how a model can be pointed at your institution's current formulary or protocols instead of whatever it absorbed during training.

technical: Retrieval that ranks documents by similarity in a learned embedding space rather than by lexical term overlap, allowing matches across paraphrase and synonymy. Dense bi-encoders embed query and document independently for fast indexing; late-interaction and cross-encoder rerankers score pairs jointly for higher accuracy at greater cost. Hybrid schemes combine dense scores with sparse lexical scores such as BM25 to recover exact-match behaviour on rare terms.
intuitive: Search that matches meaning, so a query for heart attack finds notes that say myocardial infarction. The weakness is the mirror image: it can be sloppy about exact strings such as a specific drug name or an identifier, which is why systems usually keep keyword search alongside it.
clinical: Useful for finding clinically equivalent phrasings across notes, but a purely semantic index can miss the one document containing an exact accession number.

technical: Extending a language model with external capabilities such as search, calculators, code execution, or database queries, whose results are returned into the context and conditioned on for subsequent generation. Tools offload operations that are unreliable in weights, notably exact arithmetic, current facts and authoritative lookup, converting a parametric guess into a verifiable retrieval.
intuitive: Letting the model consult instruments rather than answer from memory. A calculator gives the arithmetic, a database gives the current dose, and the model's job shifts from recalling to deciding what to look up and how to use the answer.
clinical: A model that queries a maintained drug interaction database is substantively safer than one reciting interactions from training data of unknown vintage.

technical: A store that indexes high-dimensional embedding vectors for approximate nearest-neighbour search under a similarity metric, typically cosine or inner product. Practical systems use graph-based indexes such as HNSW or quantisation-based methods to trade a small, tunable recall loss for orders-of-magnitude speedup, and usually support metadata filtering alongside vector similarity.
intuitive: A search index organised by meaning rather than by keyword, where every document is a point in space and finding relevant material means finding nearby points. It is deliberately approximate: it trades a small chance of missing the best match for the ability to search millions of documents instantly.
clinical: The retrieval layer under most clinical document assistants, and a place where protected health information is stored in a form that is not obviously readable but is still recoverable.

technical: Systematic error in model outputs that varies with a patient attribute such as race, sex, language, insurance status, or disability. It arises from label choice, sampling, measurement, and historical care patterns encoded in the training data, and it is not remedied by removing the attribute as a feature because correlated proxies remain abundant in clinical data.
intuitive: The model is reliably wrong in a particular direction for a particular group. The usual cause is not prejudice in the code but a label that quietly stands in for something else, such as using cost as a proxy for illness in a system where some patients have historically received less care.
clinical: Obermeyer showed a widely deployed population health algorithm assigned Black patients the same risk score as substantially sicker White patients, purely because it predicted future spending rather than future illness.

technical: The problem of making a model's behavior match intended human goals rather than the literal training objective. Current practice fits a reward model to human preference comparisons and optimizes the policy against it, which reliably produces outputs humans rate highly but also produces sycophancy and reward hacking, since human approval is an imperfect proxy for correctness.
intuitive: Getting the model to do what you meant instead of what you measured. The main lever today is training on what human raters preferred, which optimizes for answers that look good to a rater, and a confident wrong answer often looks better than a hedged right one.
clinical: This is the mechanism behind a model agreeing with your stated suspicion rather than challenging it, which matters most when you ask a leading question about a diagnosis you have already anchored on.

technical: A model whose input to output mapping cannot be inspected in a form a human can audit, either because of parameter count and nonlinearity or because the weights and training data are proprietary. Opacity may be technical, as in a deep network, or contractual, as in a vendor model whose feature set and development data are withheld under trade secret protection.
intuitive: You see what goes in and what comes out and nothing in between. Note that there are two separate reasons for this: the model may be too complicated to read, or the company may simply refuse to show you.
clinical: The contractual kind is the one you can actually negotiate, so procurement is the moment to ask for the feature list, the training population, and site-level performance before signing.

technical: A contract required by the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules between a covered entity and any vendor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits protected health information on its behalf. It binds the vendor to permitted uses and disclosures, security safeguards, breach notification, and subcontractor flow-down, and it makes the business associate directly liable for certain HIPAA violations.
intuitive: The contract that legally lets a vendor touch patient data and puts them on the hook if they mishandle it. Without one signed, sending identified data to that vendor is itself the violation, regardless of how secure their systems happen to be.
clinical: Consumer tiers of general-purpose AI products are typically not covered by a BAA even when the enterprise tier is, which is the single most common way clinicians create a reportable disclosure by pasting a note into a chatbot.

technical: A training method in which a model critiques and revises its own outputs against an explicit written set of principles, and those AI-generated preferences replace much of the human labeling used in reinforcement learning from human feedback. The behavioral specification becomes an auditable document rather than being implicit in a labeling contractor's guidelines.
intuitive: Instead of paying people to rate thousands of answers as acceptable or not, you write down the rules and have the model grade itself against them. The advantage is that the rules are a text you can read and argue with.
clinical: It is the reason a general-purpose assistant may refuse or heavily hedge on dosing and diagnosis questions, and those refusal behaviors are set by a published policy document rather than by anything specific to medicine.

technical: The process of rendering health information not individually identifiable, which under the HIPAA Privacy Rule is achieved by one of exactly two routes: Safe Harbor removal of eighteen enumerated identifier types, or Expert Determination in which a qualified statistician documents that reidentification risk is very small. Data meeting either standard falls outside the Privacy Rule, which is why the determination is consequential.
intuitive: Making data legally no longer about a specific person. There are only two accepted ways to do it, and running a regex over the note is not one of them unless it actually removes all eighteen categories.
clinical: Research and quality projects often depend on the claim that data is de-identified, and if the method was neither Safe Harbor nor a documented expert determination, the IRB exemption and the vendor data-sharing terms both rest on nothing.

technical: Post hoc methods that produce a human-readable account of a specific prediction from a model that is not itself transparent, typically by local surrogate fitting (LIME), Shapley value attribution (SHAP), or gradient-based attribution. Such explanations approximate the model rather than describe it, they can be unstable to small input changes, and they can be constructed to look plausible while being unfaithful to the computation performed.
intuitive: A second system that tells a story about why the first system said what it said. The story is a reconstruction, not a readout, and a reconstruction can be convincing and wrong at the same time.
clinical: Explanations reliably increase clinician confidence in model output without reliably increasing accuracy, so a tool that shows its reasoning may make you more willing to follow it when it is wrong.

technical: Most AI-enabled medical devices reach the United States market through 510(k) premarket notification, which establishes substantial equivalence to a legally marketed predicate device rather than independently demonstrating clinical benefit. Clearance is distinct from premarket approval, which is reserved for high-risk Class III devices, and from De Novo classification, which creates a new device type where no predicate exists.
intuitive: Cleared usually means the manufacturer convinced FDA the product is similar enough to something already on the market, not that a trial showed it helps patients. It is a comparison to a predecessor, and predecessors can chain back to devices validated decades ago.
clinical: The clearance summary tells you the intended use, the population studied, and the imaging or data conditions tested, and a tool used outside those conditions is off-label even though nobody will stop you.

technical: A family of formal criteria constraining how model behavior may differ across groups, including demographic parity, equalized odds, and calibration within groups. Except in degenerate cases these criteria are mutually incompatible, so choosing a fairness definition is a normative decision about which harm matters most, not a technical optimization that can be delegated to the vendor.
intuitive: There is no single mathematical definition of fair, and the plausible ones provably contradict each other. Equal false negative rates across groups and equal predictive value across groups cannot both hold when disease prevalence differs, so someone has to decide which one the tool should satisfy.
clinical: When a vendor says their model was audited for fairness, the useful follow-up is which metric they equalized and across which groups, because equalizing one of them necessarily unequalizes another.

technical: One of the two de-identification methods in the HIPAA Privacy Rule, requiring removal of eighteen specified identifier categories including names, all geographic subdivisions smaller than a state, all date elements more precise than year, ages over 89, contact and account numbers, biometric identifiers, and full-face images, together with no actual knowledge that the residual information could identify an individual.
intuitive: A checklist route to de-identification: strike these eighteen things and the data is legally de-identified. It is mechanical and defensible, but it is also blunt, because dropping all dates below the year often destroys exactly the temporal detail a clinical model needs.
clinical: Note the catch-all: even after removing all eighteen categories, Safe Harbor fails if you actually know the remaining data could identify someone, which is a live problem for small departments and rare diseases.

technical: A design and governance requirement that a qualified human reviews or approves model output before it affects a patient. Its protective value depends on the reviewer having the information, time, and independent basis to disagree, and automation bias means that oversight measurably degrades as model accuracy and reviewer workload rise.
intuitive: A person checks the model before anything happens. This works only if checking is genuinely possible and genuinely done, and a reviewer who approves ninety-nine correct outputs in a row is not meaningfully reviewing the hundredth.
clinical: Regulatory exemptions, malpractice posture, and vendor risk transfer all lean on the clinician being an independent check, so the oversight you are credited with is oversight you are also liable for.

technical: The property of a model whose decision function can be inspected and reasoned about directly, as in sparse linear models, short decision lists, or generalized additive models. It is a property of the model itself rather than of an accompanying explanation system, and for much structured clinical data the accuracy cost relative to opaque models is small or absent.
intuitive: You can read the model and see what it does, the way you can read a risk score with six weighted criteria. This is different from having a black box plus a narrator, and it is the only version where the account you are given is guaranteed to be the actual reasoning.
clinical: For tabular clinical prediction the accuracy gap between an interpretable model and a black box is usually negligible, so accepting opacity often buys nothing while costing your ability to spot a nonsense feature.

technical: A structured document accompanying a model that states intended use, out-of-scope uses, training and evaluation data provenance, and performance disaggregated across relevant subpopulations rather than reported only in aggregate. Health-specific analogues such as MINIMAR add requirements for study population, data source, and model architecture reporting.
intuitive: A spec sheet for a model: what it is for, what it was trained on, where it was tested, and how it performs in each group rather than only on average. Aggregate numbers hide the subgroups where a tool fails.
clinical: Ask for one during procurement; a vendor who cannot state the training population and subgroup performance is telling you something useful about how carefully the tool was evaluated.

technical: A section of a marketing submission that specifies, in advance, the modifications a manufacturer may make to an authorized AI-enabled device, the validation methods that will support each modification, and the assessment of resulting risk. An authorized PCCP allows those enumerated changes to be implemented without a new marketing submission, which is the regulatory mechanism for models that are retrained after clearance.
intuitive: A pre-agreed list of ways the model is allowed to change after approval, plus the testing the company promised to run each time. It exists because a model that gets retrained every quarter is not the same product that was cleared, and regulators needed a way to handle that without re-reviewing it every quarter.
clinical: Ask a vendor whether their authorization includes a PCCP and what it permits, because that is the difference between a frozen model you can characterize once and a moving target whose behavior may shift between your validation and your next audit.

technical: Individually identifiable health information held or transmitted by a covered entity or business associate in any form. Identifiability is not limited to name and medical record number; free text, dates, geography, device identifiers, and rare diagnoses can all render a record identifiable, and machine learning has been shown to reidentify individuals in datasets from which the enumerated identifiers were removed.
intuitive: Health information that can be tied back to a person, which is a much wider net than the obvious identifiers. A narrative with an admission date, a zip code, and an unusual condition is identifiable even with the name struck out.
clinical: Copying a de-named progress note into an unapproved tool is still a disclosure of PHI if dates, rare findings, or free-text detail remain, which they almost always do.

technical: Software intended for a medical purpose that performs that purpose without being part of a hardware medical device. Regulatory risk classification depends jointly on the significance of the information the software provides to a healthcare decision and on the seriousness of the patient condition, which together determine the evidence required for market authorization.
intuitive: Software that is itself the medical device, rather than firmware inside a pump or a scanner. Whether it faces light or heavy regulation depends on how sick the patient is and how much weight the output carries, not on the sophistication of the code.
clinical: If a vendor tells you their tool is not a device, ask what intended-use claim supports that, because marketing language that drifts toward diagnosis is what moves a product into device territory and into your liability.

technical: The algorithm for computing gradients of a scalar loss with respect to every parameter by applying the chain rule backwards through the computational graph, reusing intermediate results so total cost is roughly that of one forward pass. It is a gradient computation method, not an optimization method, and it supplies the gradients that gradient descent consumes. Memory scales with the activations stored during the forward pass, which is why activation checkpointing matters at scale.
intuitive: The bookkeeping that works out how much each individual parameter contributed to the error, by tracing the error backwards through the layers. Without it there would be no efficient way to know which of billions of numbers to adjust.

technical: The condition in which outcome classes occur at very different base rates, so a classifier minimizing average loss is driven toward the majority class. With prevalence p, the trivial always-negative classifier achieves accuracy 1 minus p, making accuracy uninformative for small p. Mitigations include resampling, class-weighted or focal losses, and threshold selection on a validation set; evaluation should use precision-recall curves and calibration rather than ROC alone, since ROC is insensitive to prevalence while positive predictive value is not.
intuitive: Most things worth predicting in medicine are rare, and rarity breaks the obvious scoreboard. If in-hospital cardiac arrest occurs in 1 of 200 admissions, a model that says no every single time is 99.5 percent accurate and completely useless. The number that actually matters to you is different: of the patients this model flags, what fraction truly have the condition, and that number collapses as prevalence falls even when sensitivity and specificity look excellent.
clinical: Sepsis, arrest, and rare-disease models all live here, and a vendor quoting accuracy or even AUROC without positive predictive value at the deployed threshold and local prevalence has told you almost nothing about alert burden.

technical: Applying label-preserving transformations to training examples so the model sees more variation than the raw dataset contains. Typical image transforms include rotation, flipping, cropping, and intensity jitter; text analogues include paraphrase and back-translation. Augmentation acts as a regularizer by encoding invariances the modeler believes should hold, which means a badly chosen transform teaches a false invariance.
intuitive: Showing the model the same case many times under different conditions, the way a resident learns to recognize a rash across skin tones, lighting, and camera angles. The catch is that you are asserting which changes should not matter. Flipping a chest radiograph left to right creates a normal-looking image that is actually a dextrocardia case, so the transform must respect the medicine.
clinical: Imaging models are almost always trained with augmentation, and inappropriate transforms are a quiet source of clinically wrong invariances such as ignoring laterality.

technical: The documented chain of origin, licensing, consent basis, and transformation history for every corpus used to build a model. Provenance determines whether training was legally and ethically permitted, whether evaluation sets are contaminated by overlap with training data, and whether a known-bad source can be traced and excised. Large web-scraped corpora are frequently assembled by aggregation, and audits have found license and origin metadata to be wrong or missing at high rates.
intuitive: Knowing where the training data actually came from, who consented to it, and what happened to it along the way. Without this you cannot answer basic questions such as whether the model was trained on your institution's notes, whether the benchmark it scored well on was already in its training set, or whether a source you now consider unreliable can be removed.
clinical: If a vendor cannot describe the provenance of its training corpus, you cannot assess contamination of the benchmarks they cite or verify that patient data was used within its permitted purpose.

technical: A formal guarantee on an algorithm, not a property of a dataset. A mechanism is epsilon-differentially private if the distribution over its outputs changes by at most a factor of exp(epsilon) when any single individual is added to or removed from the input. In machine learning it is usually achieved by clipping per-example gradients and adding calibrated noise, as in DP-SGD, and reported as a pair (epsilon, delta) where delta bounds the probability the guarantee fails outright.
intuitive: A mathematical promise that the result would have come out nearly the same whether or not your chart was included, which bounds how much anyone can learn specifically about you. The strength of the promise lives entirely in the epsilon value: small epsilon is a real guarantee, and large epsilon is a number on a slide. It protects individuals against inference, and it does not make the underlying data safe to release, prevent a model from being wrong, or say anything about group-level harms.
clinical: When a data-sharing proposal claims differential privacy, the only substantive questions are what epsilon and delta are, and at what unit the guarantee applies, per record or per patient across many encounters.

technical: An alignment method that optimizes a language model directly on pairwise preference data using a closed-form objective, eliminating the separate reward model and the reinforcement learning loop of RLHF. It exploits the fact that the optimal policy under a KL-regularized reward objective can be expressed analytically in terms of the policy itself, turning alignment into a simple classification-style loss. It is markedly simpler and more stable to train, with broadly comparable results on standard preference benchmarks.
intuitive: A simpler way to get the same effect as RLHF. Instead of building a separate scoring model and running reinforcement learning, it trains directly on pairs of preferred and rejected answers.

technical: Training a smaller student model to match the outputs of a larger teacher, typically by minimizing divergence from the teacher's full output distribution rather than only the hard labels. The soft targets carry information about relative class similarities, which acts as a strong regularizer and lets the student approach teacher performance at a fraction of the compute. Sequence-level variants simply fine-tune the student on text generated by the teacher.
intuitive: A big expensive model teaches a small cheap one by showing not just the right answer but how confident it was in each alternative. The small model inherits much of the behavior, and also inherits the teacher's mistakes and biases.
clinical: Most small models that can run inside a hospital firewall are distilled from larger ones, so validating the teacher tells you little about the student you actually deployed.

technical: One complete pass of the optimizer over the training dataset. Conventional supervised training runs many epochs with early stopping monitored on a validation set, whereas large language model pretraining is typically near single-epoch because the corpus exceeds what the compute budget can revisit. In data-constrained settings, repeating data for a few epochs is nearly as effective as fresh data, with returns decaying rapidly beyond roughly four passes.
intuitive: One full read-through of the training set. Small models read the data many times; the largest models often see most of their data only once because there is so much of it.
clinical: Repeated epochs on a small institutional dataset are a common route to memorizing individual patient records, which is both an overfitting and a privacy problem.

technical: A distributed training scheme in which each site computes model updates on its local data and transmits only those updates to a coordinator, which aggregates them into a shared global model. The canonical algorithm is federated averaging. It removes the need to pool raw records, but the transmitted gradients are functions of the local data and can leak substantial information about it; formal privacy requires layering secure aggregation and differential privacy on top.
intuitive: The model travels to each hospital instead of the data traveling to the model. Each site trains on its own patients and sends back only what it learned, which is then averaged across sites. What is critical to understand is that raw data staying home is a governance and logistics win, not a mathematical privacy guarantee, because the updates themselves can be inverted to reconstruct training examples unless additional protections are added.
clinical: This is the architecture behind most multi-institution model-building proposals, and vendors routinely describe it as privacy-preserving when unprotected federated learning is merely data-minimizing.

technical: Continued training of a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific or domain-specific dataset, usually at a much lower learning rate. It may update all parameters or only a small added subset, as in parameter-efficient methods. The characteristic risks are catastrophic forgetting of pretrained capabilities and overfitting to a narrow dataset.
intuitive: Taking a model that already knows language in general and giving it focused additional training on your specific task or data. Much cheaper than training from scratch, but pushing too hard on a narrow dataset makes the model worse at everything else.
clinical: A model fine-tuned on one health system's notes often degrades at another, because it has absorbed local documentation habits as if they were medicine.

technical: An iterative optimization procedure that updates parameters in the direction of the negative gradient of the loss, scaled by a learning rate. Stochastic variants estimate the gradient from minibatches, which is both computationally necessary at scale and a source of useful regularizing noise. Adaptive methods such as Adam maintain per-parameter running estimates of gradient moments and are standard for transformer training, usually with warmup and decay schedules on the learning rate.
intuitive: Training works by repeatedly nudging every parameter slightly in whichever direction reduces the error, a bit like walking downhill in fog by always stepping in the steepest downward direction. Millions of tiny steps eventually reach a good enough valley, though not provably the best one.

technical: Fine-tuning a base model on a large collection of tasks reformatted as natural-language instructions with responses, so the model learns to generalize to instructions it has never seen. It substantially improves zero-shot performance relative to the base model and is the step that converts a text continuer into an assistant. Instruction data may be human-written, templated from existing datasets, or generated by a stronger model.
intuitive: Training the model on many tasks phrased as instructions so it learns the general habit of doing what it is told. This is why a chat model answers your question instead of writing three more questions like it.

technical: A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that freezes the pretrained weights and learns a low-rank update, expressed as the product of two thin matrices, added to selected weight matrices. This reduces trainable parameters and optimizer memory by orders of magnitude, and the learned update can be merged into the base weights at inference so latency is unchanged. Multiple task-specific adapters can be swapped over a single shared base model.
intuitive: Instead of retraining all of a model's billions of numbers, you freeze them and learn a small patch that adjusts the behavior. The patch is tiny, cheap to train, and can be swapped out per task.
clinical: It makes specialty-specific or site-specific adaptation feasible on modest hardware, including on premises where protected health information cannot leave the institution.

technical: The scalar function of model outputs and targets that training minimizes, defining what the model is actually optimized for. Language models are trained with token-level cross-entropy, equivalent to maximizing the log likelihood of the observed text, and perplexity is its exponential. The loss is a proxy for the goal, so any mismatch between loss and intended behavior is a source of systematic failure, which is the underlying reason alignment stages exist.
intuitive: The single number that measures how wrong the model is, which training tries to make as small as possible. Whatever that number rewards is what the model becomes good at, so a badly chosen loss produces a model that is excellent at the wrong thing.
clinical: A model optimized for average accuracy will happily trade away sensitivity on a rare but lethal diagnosis, because the loss never encoded that asymmetry in harm.

technical: The regime in which a model fits noise and idiosyncrasies of the training set, so training loss continues to fall while held-out loss rises. Classical bias-variance reasoning predicts this worsens monotonically with capacity, but very large models exhibit double descent, where test error falls again past the interpolation threshold. Standard mitigations are more or more diverse data, weight decay, dropout, early stopping and augmentation.
intuitive: The model memorizes the training examples instead of learning the pattern, so it looks excellent on the data it was built from and disappoints on anything new. This is why performance must always be reported on data the model has never seen.
clinical: A model can reach superb internal accuracy by keying on a scanner artifact or a local documentation quirk, then fail entirely at another hospital.

technical: The initial, most expensive training phase in which a model learns general representations from a very large unlabeled corpus using a self-supervised objective such as next-token prediction or masked token prediction. It requires no human annotation, which is what allows the corpus to reach trillions of tokens. The resulting base model has broad knowledge but is not aligned to follow instructions or to refuse harmful requests.
intuitive: The long, costly phase where the model reads an enormous amount of text and learns language and world knowledge by predicting what comes next. A model straight out of pretraining continues text rather than answering questions.
clinical: Whatever medical knowledge a model has comes mostly from this phase, so it reflects the internet's medical content, with its errors and its publication date, not a curated guideline set.

technical: Representing weights and sometimes activations at reduced numeric precision, commonly 8-bit or 4-bit integers instead of 16-bit floats, to cut memory footprint and bandwidth. Post-training quantization calibrates scales on a small dataset without retraining, while quantization-aware training simulates the rounding during fine-tuning. Careful handling of outlier activation channels is what allows large models to be quantized with minimal loss in perplexity.
intuitive: Storing the model's numbers with less precision, like rounding to two decimal places instead of eight. The model gets several times smaller and faster with usually small quality loss, though rare edge cases can degrade more than benchmarks suggest.
clinical: The quantized version you can afford to run locally is not the same artifact that was validated, so accuracy claims from the full-precision model do not automatically transfer.

technical: An alignment procedure in which human comparisons between model outputs train a reward model, and the language model is then optimized against that reward with a policy gradient method such as PPO, regularized by a KL penalty toward the supervised model. It optimizes a learned proxy for human preference rather than truth, so it is vulnerable to reward hacking and to sycophancy. It reliably improves helpfulness and harmlessness ratings while sometimes reducing calibration.
intuitive: Humans rank pairs of model answers, a second model learns to predict those rankings, and the main model is then trained to score well on that predictor. The model is therefore taught to produce answers people like, which is not the same as answers that are right.
clinical: This training pressure is a major source of agreeable, confident answers, so a model may soften or abandon a correct assessment when a clinician pushes back.

technical: Empirical power-law relationships in which test loss falls predictably with increases in parameters, training tokens and compute, over many orders of magnitude. The compute-optimal frontier specifies how to trade parameters against tokens for a fixed budget, and the Chinchilla analysis showed that models of the era were substantially undertrained relative to their size. Scaling laws predict loss, not downstream capability, and the mapping from loss to useful behavior remains poorly characterized.
intuitive: The observation that making models bigger and feeding them more data improves them in a smooth, predictable way. It tells you how much better the next model will be at predicting text, not what new things it will be able to do.

technical: Fine-tuning on curated prompt and response pairs with a standard next-token cross-entropy loss, so the model imitates demonstrated outputs. It is the first stage of the usual post-training pipeline and establishes format, tone and instruction-following before any preference optimization. Data quality dominates data quantity, and a few thousand carefully written examples can outperform far larger noisy sets.
intuitive: Showing the model many worked examples of a question and a good answer, and training it to reproduce that style of answer. It teaches the model how to respond, not whether the content is correct.
clinical: This stage is what makes a model sound like a confident consultant, which is precisely why fluency should not be read as evidence of accuracy.

technical: Records produced by a generative model or simulator that are fitted to the statistical structure of a real dataset rather than drawn from it directly. Utility is measured by whether models trained on synthetic data transfer to real data, and privacy is measured by resistance to membership inference and attribute inference attacks. The two objectives trade off: synthetic data that preserves rare joint distributions well is also the kind most likely to memorize the individuals who produced them.
intuitive: A fabricated patient cohort built to have the same shape as a real one, so it can be shared or used for testing without handing over the original charts. It is not automatically anonymous. If a generator has seen exactly one 34 year old with a rare mitochondrial disorder, the synthetic record it emits for that phenotype may effectively be that person.
clinical: Vendors increasingly offer synthetic EHR extracts as a way around data use agreements, but synthetic does not mean de-identified and does not by itself discharge HIPAA or IRB obligations.

technical: Partitioning data into a set used to fit parameters, a set used to select hyperparameters and stopping points, and a set touched only once for the final unbiased performance estimate. The estimate is unbiased only if the partition respects the dependence structure of the data: splitting by row rather than by patient, site, or time leaks information across the boundary. Repeated evaluation on the test set converts it into a second validation set and reinflates the reported performance.
intuitive: Three separate piles of data with three separate jobs: one to learn from, one to tune against, and one that stays sealed until the very end. The most common way this goes wrong in clinical work is splitting by encounter instead of by patient, so the same person appears on both sides and the model gets credit for recognizing an individual rather than a disease. Splitting at random across time is a subtler version of the same error, since it lets the model learn from the future.
clinical: Ask any model developer how they split, and treat patient-level plus temporal or site-level splitting as the minimum bar before believing a reported performance figure.

technical: The presence of evaluation items, or near duplicates of them, in a model's training corpus, which inflates benchmark scores without any corresponding gain in capability. Web-scale pretraining makes it nearly unavoidable for any public benchmark, and n-gram overlap checks detect only verbatim leakage, missing paraphrases and translations. Credible evaluation therefore requires held-out sets created after the training cutoff or kept private.
intuitive: The exam questions were in the textbook the model studied. Its impressive score reflects recall of the answer key rather than the ability to reason through a new case.
clinical: Published board-exam and USMLE-style results are the clearest example, since those question banks are all over the internet, so such scores say little about performance on your next undifferentiated patient.

technical: Embedding a statistically detectable signal into model output so that a party holding the detection key can test whether text or an image was machine generated. For language models this is typically done at decoding time by pseudorandomly partitioning the vocabulary at each step and biasing sampling toward one partition, which yields a hypothesis test with a computable p-value. Watermarks degrade under paraphrase, translation, and heavy editing, and they say nothing about output from unwatermarked models.
intuitive: A hidden fingerprint deliberately woven into generated text or images so it can later be identified as machine produced. It only works if the generating system chose to add it, and it can be washed out by rewriting. So a positive detection is meaningful evidence, while a negative detection is close to worthless, which is the opposite of how it is usually marketed.
clinical: Relevant to documentation integrity and academic honesty policies, but a watermark absence cannot be used to certify that a note or manuscript was human written.
